cultivar: Mixed Chinese-origin (sinensis) plants raised from the estate's own cuttings and seed, chosen for cold tolerance
processing: Small-batch orthodox black tea: hand-picked leaf withered, rolled, oxidised and dried on the estate; the pure single-estate tea is sold on its own, while the estate's everyday blends combine a small share of Cornish leaf with imported Assam, Darjeeling and Ceylon.
harvest_season: A short season from late spring to early autumn (roughly May to September), with the first spring pick the finest; the bushes are dormant through the Cornish winter.
appearance_dry: Fine, dark, slightly uneven twisted leaves with a few tips, in small quantities; the blends look like standard broken black tea.
appearance_liquor: Light amber, clear, pale for a black tea.
taste_profile: Light, delicate and faintly floral with hay, a gentle malt and a sweet, clean finish, low in tannin; the single-estate tea is closer to a light Darjeeling than to an English breakfast cup, and the blends taste like good mainstream black tea.

brewing.notes: Treat the single-estate tea gently: water a little off the boil, two and a half minutes, no milk. The blends take boiling water, three to four minutes and milk in the usual English way.

vintage_note: The pure Cornish single-estate tea is sold in tiny quantities, by the season and year, in small tins or caddies at a very high price per gram, and sells out; the estate's branded blends (Classic, Afternoon, Earl Grey and others) are sold year-round in bags and loose and are not dated. Drink either within a year or two.
description:
Tregothnan is the estate that gave England a tea garden. The Boscawen family's land on the Fal estuary near Truro has grown ornamental camellias since the nineteenth century, and in the late 1990s the estate planted Camellia sinensis in the same sheltered, frost-light valley, reasoning that if the ornamental cousins thrived, tea would too. The first harvest was sold in 2005, with a great deal of press about the 'first English tea'.

The plantation is small and the climate is marginal, so the pure Cornish tea is made in tiny batches, hand-picked from late spring, rolled and oxidised on the estate, and sold at prices that reflect scarcity rather than flavour. The estate's main business is a range of branded teas, Classic, Afternoon, Earl Grey and infusions, in which a small proportion of Cornish leaf is blended with imported Assam, Darjeeling and Ceylon; those are the teas most people have actually drunk under the Tregothnan name.

The single-estate tea is light and delicate, faintly floral with hay, a gentle malt and a sweet finish, and low in tannin; it is nearer to a light Darjeeling than to a builder's brew, and it needs gentle brewing and no milk. The blends are good mainstream black teas and taste like it. Expect novelty and place rather than depth from the pure tea, and judge the blends as blends.

Buy with your eyes open: read the label to see whether you are getting the 100% Cornish tea or a blend, since both carry the estate name and the price gap is enormous. The pure tea is sold by season in small tins from the estate and a few London shops; the blends are everywhere from the estate's website to department stores. Tea is also grown on a tiny scale elsewhere in Britain, in Scotland, Wales and other English gardens, but Tregothnan is the best known.

If the idea of cold-climate tea interests you, the Krasnodar and Georgian teas of the Black Sea and the Azores' Gorreana are the other European gardens worth tasting beside it.
sources_note: First planting (1999) and first sale (2005) are from memory of press coverage. The proportion of Cornish leaf in the estate's blends is not published and is described only as 'a small share'. Scottish tea growers were considered for a separate card and omitted for lack of confidence after the publicised fraud case involving one 'Scottish tea' supplier.
history:
Tregothnan, near Truro in Cornwall, was home to the first outdoor camellias in Britain, around 1800. The first tea plants went into the Kitchen Garden in 1999, though that spot proved unsuitable for expansion.

The first commercial tea was developed in 2001, and the first 'English tea' was sold to Fortnum & Mason in November 2005. Jonathon Jones, the botanist who ran the trading side, researched the project on site and in other tea regions with a Nuffield Scholarship.

Over 20,000 more bushes are reported going in each year, though the figure is undated, and the project drew wide media interest.
